meta.ogDescription: A line about rations of slavery that Tocqueville never wrote. It is P. J. O’Rourke, from The Liberty Manifesto, delivered at the Cato Institute in May 1993.

answer.label: Not Tocqueville — P. J. O’Rourke, 1993
answer.sourceLine: This is modern American libertarian satire, not nineteenth-century French political sociology. Wikiquote files it under Misattributed on its Tocqueville page and credits it to P. J. O’Rourke, Age and Guile Beat Youth, Innocence, and a Bad Haircut (1996), p. 227 the entry ↗. Wikiquote’s separate O’Rourke page carries the same passage under The Liberty Manifesto, a speech delivered on 6 May 1993 for the opening of the Cato Institute’s Washington headquarters the O’Rourke entry ↗ — and the book is an anthology of his work from 1970 to 1995, so a 1993 speech reprinted at p. 227 fits. Two vocabulary items alone rule Tocqueville out: he died in 1859, and neither ‘health care’ nor ‘housing’ existed as a claimed right in his lifetime.

source.heading: The source

Age and Guile Beat Youth, Innocence, and a Bad Haircut (New York: Atlantic Monthly Press), p. 227
Democracy in America — absent from both volumes

source.excerpt: Freedom is not empowerment. Empowerment is what the Serbs have in Bosnia. Anybody can grab a gun and be empowered. It's not entitlement. An entitlement is what people on welfare get, and how free are they? It's not an endlessly expanding list of rights — the "right" to education, the "right" to food and housing. That's not freedom, that's dependency. Those aren't rights, those are the rations of slavery — hay and a barn for human cattle.
trail: Both halves come from Wikiquote, and they agree. The Tocqueville page lists the passage as misattributed and points to O’Rourke’s Age and Guile Beat Youth, Innocence, and a Bad Haircut (1996), p. 227 Tocqueville, Misattributed ↗. The O’Rourke page, compiled separately, carries the same words in their paragraph under The Liberty Manifesto, dated 6 May 1993 and placed at the opening of the Cato Institute’s headquarters O’Rourke, The Liberty Manifesto ↗.

The book and the speech are consistent. Age and Guile is an anthology subtitled ‘twenty-five years of P. J. O’Rourke, 1970–1995’, published in New York by Atlantic Monthly Press in 1995 with a 1996 printing — so a speech from 1993 appearing on p. 227 is exactly what an anthology of that span would contain the 1996 Atlantic Monthly Press edition ↗.

It is not in Tocqueville. Neither ‘rations of slavery’ nor ‘human cattle’ nor anything about an expanding list of rights appears in the searchable Reeve translation of Democracy in America volume one ↗ volume two ↗.

The paragraph dates itself. It measures empowerment against ‘what the Serbs have in Bosnia’ and entitlement against ‘what people on welfare get’ — comparisons that belong to the 1990s and to nothing earlier his life and affiliations ↗. He lived 1947–2022.
source.cutTag: P. J. O’Rourke, The Liberty Manifesto, 6 May 1993
source.excerptNote: The passage in its full paragraph, as Wikiquote transcribes it from the speech the transcription ↗. Read it beside the version at the top of this page and one difference stands out: the circulating ‘Tocqueville’ text inserts the ‘right’ to health care into the list, which this transcription does not contain. We could not open p. 227 of the book to see whether O’Rourke added the clause when he reprinted it, so we record the discrepancy without explaining it. The reference to Bosnia in the opening sentence dates the paragraph on its own: the Serbs were not in Bosnia in 1835.

source.rightsNote: This one is genuinely in copyright, and the misattribution obscures that. A speech given in 1993 and collected in a book first published in 1995 is protected in the United States for the author’s life plus seventy years, so quoting it at length is a permissions question, not a public-domain one. Attributing it to a Frenchman who died in 1859 makes it look free to reproduce when it is not — which is one practical reason a false attribution is worth correcting. Short quotation with attribution to O’Rourke is the ordinary practice. This is not legal advice.

author.name: P. J. O’Rourke
author.heading: About P. J. O’Rourke
author.metaLine: 1947–2022 · American satirist, journalist and libertarian humorist
author.bio: Patrick Jake O’Rourke went from editing the National Lampoon in the 1970s to reporting from far-flung places as Rolling Stone’s foreign-affairs desk chief, and to writing twenty-two books, two of which — Parliament of Whores and Give War a Chance — reached number one on the New York Times bestseller list. He delivered The Liberty Manifesto at the opening of the Cato Institute’s Washington headquarters in May 1993. His register is the reason the misattribution works at all: the sentence has the cadence of a nineteenth-century moralist and the content of a very twentieth-century joke, and readers who notice the first often miss the second.

misattribution.heading: Attributed to the wrong man, and altered on the way
misattribution.intro: Two things happened to this passage. It was reassigned from a living American satirist to a dead French aristocrat, and somewhere in the process it grew a clause.

items.why: Wikiquote lists it under Misattributed on his page and names O’Rourke as the source the entry ↗. Nothing resembling it is in Democracy in America volume two ↗, and Tocqueville died in 1859.

From The Liberty Manifesto, delivered 6 May 1993 at the opening of the Cato Institute’s headquarters in Washington and collected in Age and Guile Beat Youth, Innocence, and a Bad Haircut at p. 227 the speech ↗.

items.tag: not in the transcription we read
items.why: The version circulating under Tocqueville’s name lists education, health care, and food and housing. The transcription of the speech on Wikiquote’s O’Rourke page lists only education, and food and housing the transcription ↗. We could not open p. 227 of the book to check whether the printed text differs from the spoken one, so we flag the discrepancy without resolving it.

The sentences immediately before the quoted portion measure empowerment against what ‘the Serbs have in Bosnia’ and entitlement against ‘what people on welfare get’. Both belong to 1993. Neither belongs to 1835.

misattribution.truthLine: It is P. J. O’Rourke, from The Liberty Manifesto, delivered at the Cato Institute on 6 May 1993 and reprinted in Age and Guile Beat Youth, Innocence, and a Bad Haircut, p. 227 the source ↗.

context.heading: Why the swap happened
lead: The passage is an argument against positive rights, and quoting it is a political act. Under O’Rourke’s name it is one American humorist’s opinion, delivered to a think-tank audience at a building opening, and you are free to find it funny or offensive. Under Tocqueville’s it becomes a historical verdict on the American republic delivered by its most famous foreign analyst.

That upgrade is the whole point of the misattribution, and it is why this one is worth correcting even though nobody is being defamed. The words are not in dispute; only their weight is, and the weight is entirely borrowed.
detailsBody: 1859: Tocqueville dies. Democracy in America contains nothing of the kind.
6 May 1993: P. J. O’Rourke delivers The Liberty Manifesto at the opening of the Cato Institute’s Washington headquarters.
1995–1996: the speech is collected in Age and Guile Beat Youth, Innocence, and a Bad Haircut (New York: Atlantic Monthly Press) at p. 227.
Later: the passage begins circulating under Tocqueville’s name, with the ‘right’ to health care added to the list.
Wikiquote records the misattribution on the Tocqueville page and the genuine text on the O’Rourke page.
context.pull: Under O’Rourke’s name it is a joke with a thesis. Under Tocqueville’s it is a prophecy.
